beats.narration: Eleven at night. Sprout Pro reboots, roughly once every two hours, for no visible reason. The display goes blank, the light flickers, and it starts again, as if nothing happened.
It never happens when the debugger is attached. Never. I have been watching it for six hours.
Investor day is in two weeks! Can we just hide the reboot? Maybe make it look like a feature? A little nap?
No. A device that reboots randomly is a device that someday reboots with the pump on, or loses a settings write halfway. We find it.
This episode is about the bugs that seem impossible: crashes that vanish under observation, code that works until you turn on optimization, and the hard faults that stop a processor cold.
First clue. Ben's debug build, with optimization off, never crashes. The release build, with optimization on, does. Cy immediately blames the compiler.

title.sub: The Optimizer Is Not Your Enemy

beats.narration: Turn off the optimizer. Problem solved.
The optimizer is almost never the bug. It is the thing that reveals the bug. Optimized code is smaller and faster, and it takes the language rules literally.
Here, a variable is changed by an interrupt, but it is not marked volatile.

visual.title: What the optimizer saw
lines: bool tank_empty = false;             // set by an interrupt

beats.narration: The compiler sees a loop that never modifies it, so it reads it once and loops forever, or skips the loop entirely. Both are legal.

visual.title: What the optimizer saw
lines: bool tank_empty = false;             // set by an interrupt

beats.narration: The language promises that a normal variable only changes when your code changes it.

visual.title: What the optimizer saw
lines: bool tank_empty = false;             // set by an interrupt

beats.narration: Interrupts, hardware registers, and other tasks break that promise, so you must tell the compiler, with volatile, or with proper synchronization.

visual.title: What the optimizer saw
lines: bool tank_empty = false;             // set by an interrupt

beats.narration: Timing loops too. A delay that counts to a million does nothing useful, so the optimizer removes it. Suddenly the sensor gets asked too early.

visual.title: Things optimization exposes
items: Missing volatile on shared variables
Reading uninitialized variables
Undefined behavior, like signed overflow
Timing loops that the compiler deletes
Code that relied on a lucky memory layout

beats.narration: And undefined behavior: overflowing a signed integer, reading past an array, using a pointer after freeing it. Unoptimized code often does something reasonable by accident.

beats.narration: The lesson is to build with optimization on early, test that build, and treat any difference between debug and release as a bug in your code, not in the compiler.

beats.narration: Ada adds volatile to the tank flag. The reboots slow down, but do not stop. Now it is once every five hours. That is the worst kind of progress.
When a bug seems impossible, one of your assumptions is wrong. The job is to find which one. So we stop guessing, and we collect facts.

Make it reproducible on demand
Change one thing at a time
Explain it fully before you fix it

beats.narration: Fact one: it only reboots while the display is refreshing. Fact two: it is worse when the history log is long. Fact three: never with the debugger attached.

beats.narration: The reboot is not a power glitch.
Ada finds it is the processor hitting a hard fault: a condition so wrong that the processor refuses to continue, jumps to a fault handler, and, in Sprout's code, the fault handler resets the chip.
On processors like Sprout's, many errors that would print a message on a laptop instead cause a fault.

visual.title: Common hard fault causes
items: Dereferencing a bad pointer
Writing past the end of the stack
Misaligned memory access
Executing from invalid memory
Dividing by zero, if trapping is on
Calling an invalid function pointer

beats.narration: A null pointer, a corrupted function pointer, an access to memory that does not exist.

beats.narration: Stack overflow is a sneaky one. The stack grows downward as functions call functions.

beats.narration: If it grows too far, it silently tramples whatever sits below it in RAM, often global variables. Nothing complains until some trampled value causes chaos later.

beats.narration: The display buffer sits right below the stack. If the stack overflows, it scribbles over the screen data.
Or the other way around. If the display code writes past the end of its buffer, it might corrupt something else. Let us find out exactly.
Alignment faults are another classic. Many processors require a four-byte value to start at an address divisible by four.
Code that casts a byte pointer, from the middle of a received message, into a pointer to a thirty-two bit number can trigger a fault on some chips, and silently slow access on others.
The safe way is to copy the bytes into a properly declared variable, with memcpy, instead of pretending a random address holds an aligned integer.
When a fault happens on these processors, the hardware has already saved the registers on the stack, including the address of the instruction that was running.
The fault handler can read that crime scene.
The program counter tells us where the crash happened. The link register tells us who called that code. The fault status register tells us what kind of fault it was.

visual.title: A fault handler that records evidence
lines: crash.lr   = sp[5];          // where it was called from
crash.cfsr = FAULT_STATUS;   // why: bad address? bad alignment?
>  crash.magic = 0xDEADBEEF;    // mark the record as valid

beats.narration: The record goes into a small area of RAM that the startup code is told not to clear.

beats.narration: Font draw char, writing just past the end of RAM. The display code is not the victim. It is the culprit.

beats.narration: Ada reads font draw char line by line.
The history screen draws the watering count, a number that, for long logs, has more digits than the text buffer was sized for.
The text buffer has room for six characters. A long history produces ten.

visual.title: The bug
lines: char text[6];                       // room for 5 digits + end

beats.narration: Sprintf writes past the end, overwrites the stack, and the corrupted return address sends the processor into the wilderness.

visual.title: The bug
lines: char text[6];                       // room for 5 digits + end

beats.narration: And it only happened with a long log, because only then did the number get big enough!

visual.title: The bug
lines: char text[6];                       // room for 5 digits + end

beats.narration: And the debugger? With it attached, the build used a different stack layout, so the overflow trampled something harmless. Impossible, until it is obvious.

visual.title: The bug
lines: char text[6];                       // room for 5 digits + end

beats.narration: A bigger buffer, and snprintf, which never writes more than the size you give it.

visual.title: The fix
lines: >snprintf(text, sizeof text, "%lu ml", total);   // never overflows

beats.narration: And a test: draw the history screen with the largest possible numbers, every time we build.

visual.title: The fix
lines: >snprintf(text, sizeof text, "%lu ml", total);   // never overflows

beats.narration: Two weeks to investor day, and the impossible bug is dead. I knew we would find it.

beats.narration: Ada wants more than a crash record next time. She sets up a core dump: on a fault, the device saves a snapshot of RAM and registers to flash.
Later, the snapshot is copied to a laptop and loaded into the debugger, as if the crash just happened.
With a core dump, you can inspect every variable, walk the call stack, and see exactly what the device was doing when it died, even if it died a thousand kilometers away.
And there are defenses that catch problems earlier, before they become mysteries.
The stack pattern trick is great. Fill the stack with a known value at boot. Later, see how much of the pattern was overwritten.

Keep crash records in the field

beats.narration: To recap. When a bug only appears with optimization, look for missing volatile, undefined behavior, or deleted timing loops. The optimizer is usually the messenger.

Hard faults: bad pointers, stack overflow, alignment
Record PC, LR, and fault status for the post-mortem
Core dumps and guard regions catch the rest
